# lipsum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lipsum/

## Expand description

Lorem ipsum generator.

This crate generates pseudo-Latin [lorem ipsum placeholder
text](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorem_ipsum). The traditional lorem ipsum text start like this:

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.

This text is in the [ LOREM_IPSUM](https://docs.rs/constant.LOREM_IPSUM.html) constant. Random looking text
like the above can be generated using the

[function. The function allows you to generate as much text as desired and each invocation will generate different text.](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum.html)

`lipsum`The random looking text is generated using a [Markov chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain) of
order two, which simply means that the next word is based on the
previous two words in the input texts. The Markov chain can be
used with other input texts by creating an instance of
[ MarkovChain](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html) and calling its

[method.](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html#method.learn)

`learn`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Markov](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html)- Chain
- Simple order two Markov chain implementation.
- [Words](https://docs.rs/struct.Words.html)
- Never-ending iterator over words in the Markov chain.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [LIBER_](https://docs.rs/constant.LIBER_PRIMUS.html)- PRIMUS
- The first book in Cicero’s work De finibus bonorum et malorum (“On
the ends of good and evil”). The lorem ipsum text in
`LOREM_IPSUM`
- [LOREM_](https://docs.rs/constant.LOREM_IPSUM.html)- IPSUM
- The traditional lorem ipsum text as given in [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorem_ipsum). Using this text alone for a Markov chain of order two doesn’t work very well since each bigram (two consequtive words) is followed by just one other word. In other words, the Markov chain will always produce the same output and recreate the lorem ipsum text precisely. However, combining it with the full text in`LIBER_PRIMUS`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [lipsum](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum.html)
- Generate `n`words of lorem ipsum text. The output will always start with “Lorem ipsum”.
- [lipsum_](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum_title.html)- title
- Generate a short lorem ipsum text with words in title case.
- [lipsum_](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum_title_with_rng.html)- title_ - with_ - rng
- Generate a short lorem ipsum text with words in title case with a custom RNG.
- [lipsum_](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum_with_rng.html)- with_ - rng
- Generate `n`words of lorem ipsum text with a custom RNG. The output will always start with “Lorem ipsum”.
- [lipsum_](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum_words.html)- words
- Generate `n`words of lorem ipsum text.
- [lipsum_](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum_words_with_rng.html)- words_ - with_ - rng
- Generate `n`words of lorem ipsum text with a custom RNG.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Bigram](https://docs.rs/type.Bigram.html)
- A bigram is simply two consecutive words.

# lipsum 0.9.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lipsum/latest

# Lorem Ipsum

Lipsum is a small Rust library for generating pseudo-Latin [lorem
ipsum filler text](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorem_ipsum). This is a standard placeholder text
used in publishing. It starts with:

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua. Ut enim ad minim veniam, quis nostrud exercitation ullamco laboris nisi ut aliquip ex ea commodo consequat…

The text is generated using a [Markov chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain) that has been trained on
the first book in Cicero's work *De finibus bonorum et malorum* (*On
the ends of good and evil*), of which the lorem ipsum text is a
scrambled subset.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.9"
```
## Documentation

Please see the ** API documentation**.

## Getting Started

Use the `lipsum` function to generate lorem ipsum text:

```
use lipsum;
```
This generates the lorem ipsum text show above:

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua. Ut enim ad minim veniam, quis nostrud exercitation ullamco…

The text becomes random after 18 words, so you might not see exactly the same text.

Use `lipsum_title` instead if you just need a short text suitable for
a document title or a section heading. The text generated by that
function looks like this:

Refugiendi et Omnino Rerum

Small words are kept uncapitalized and punctuation is stripped from all words.

## Release History

This is a changelog with the most important changes in each release.

### Version 0.9.1 (2024-03-13)

- [#100](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/100): Add- `lipsum_title_with_rng`function.
- [#102](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/102): Document MSRV in- `Cargo.toml`.
- [#103](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/103): Enable dependabot updates.

### Version 0.9.0 (2023-03-28)

- [#90](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/90): Test minimum supported Rust version (Rust 1.56) in CI
- [#91](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/91): Remove dependency on system randomness

### Version 0.8.2 (2022-06-06)

- [#84](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/84): Fix build error on Rust 1.56. Thanks @WorldSEnder for the report.

### Version 0.8.1 (2022-04-19)

- [#73](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/73): Add- `lipsum_from_seed`and tweak capitalization. Thanks @reknih!
- [#77](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/77): Update to Rust 2021 edition.

### Version 0.8.0 (2021-05-30)

The random number generator has been separated from the `MarkovChain`
implementation to allow using the same trained model to generate
multiple outputs with different seeds. Thanks @Diggsey!

### Version 0.7.0 (2020-07-08)

-
The code has been updated to the [Rust 2018 edition](https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2018/).
-
Each new release will only support the latest stable version of Rust. Trying to support older Rust versions has proven to be a fool's errand: our dependencies keep releasing new patch versions that require newer and newer versions of Rust.
-
[#65](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/65): A new`lipsum_words_from_seed`function was added. It generates random but deterministic lorem ipsum text. This is useful in unit tests when you need fixed inputs.

### Version 0.6.0 (2018-12-09)

The new `lipsum_words` function can be used to generate random lorem
ipsum text that doesn't always start with "Lorem ipsum".

Dependencies were updated and the oldest supported version of Rust is now 1.22.

### Version 0.5.0 (2018-04-22)

The new `lipsum_title` function can be used to generate a short string
suitable for a document title or a section heading.

Dependencies were updated and the oldest supported version of Rust is now 1.17.

### Version 0.4.0 (2017-09-24)

The `generate` and `generate_from` now always generate proper
sentences, meaning that they generate sentences that start with a
capital letter and end with `.` or some other punctuation character.
Use `iter` and `iter_from` directly if you need more control.

### Version 0.3.0 (2017-07-28)

Performance is improved by about 50% when generating text, but training the Markov chain now takes about twice as long as before.

The `MarkovChain` struct has many new methods:

-
`new_with_rng`makes it possible to specify the random number generator used by the Markov chain. Use this to get deterministic and thus reproducible output for tests.`MarkovChain`now owns the RNG it uses and as a consequence, it has an extra type parameter. This is a breaking change if you used struct directly in your code.
-
`iter`and`into_from`return iterators over words in the Markov chain. The`generate`and`generate_from`methods are now straight-forward convenience wrappers for the iterators.
-
`len`tells you the number of stats in the Markov chain and`is_empty`tells you if the Markov chain is empty, meaning that it hasn't been trained on anything yet.

### Version 0.2.0 (2017-07-10)

Rust version 1.6.0 is now supported. This is checked with TravisCI.

### Version 0.1.0 (2017-07-2)

First public release.

## License

Lipsum can be distributed according to the [MIT license](https://docs.rs/LICENSE).
Contributions will be accepted under the same license.

# lipsum 0.9.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lipsum/latest/source/

#
                    lipsum 0.9.1

                Lipsum is a lorem ipsum text generation library. It generates
pseudo-random Latin text. Use this if you need filler or dummy text
for your application.
The text is generated using a simple Markov chain, which you can
instantiate to generate your own pieces of pseudo-random text.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.5/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

- Convenience re-export of common members

- Sequence-related functionality

- Types which may be filled with random data

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- Retrieve the lazily-initialized thread-local random number generator,
seeded by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style,
e.g. `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`, or cached locally, e.g.`let mut rng = thread_rng();`. Invoked by the`Default`trait, making`ThreadRng::default()`equivalent.

# version_sync - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/version-sync/^0.9.4/

## Expand description

`version-sync` provides macros for keeping version numbers in sync
with your crate version.

[§](https://docs.rs#library-overview)Library Overview

When making a release of a Rust project, you typically need to adjust some version numbers in your code and documentation. This crate gives you macros that covers some typical cases where version numbers need updating:

-
TOML examples in the `README.md`files that show how to add a dependency on your crate. See`assert_markdown_deps_updated`
-
A `Changelog.md`file that should at least mention the current version. See`assert_contains_regex``assert_contains_substring`
-
A `README.md`file which should only mention the current version. See`assert_only_contains_regex`
-
The `html_root_url``assert_html_root_url_updated`

Except for [ assert_contains_substring](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_contains_substring.html), the macros are gated
behind individual features, as detailed below.

A typical configuration will use an integration test to verify
that all version numbers are in sync. Create a
`tests/version-numbers.rs` file with:

```
#[test]
fn test_readme_deps_updated() {
    version_sync::assert_markdown_deps_updated!("README.md");
}
#[test]
fn test_readme_mentions_version() {
    version_sync::assert_contains_substring!("README.md", "Version {version}");
}
#[test]
fn test_html_root_url() {
    version_sync::assert_html_root_url_updated!("src/lib.rs");
}
```
When you run `cargo test`, your version numbers will be
automatically checked.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

In case you only need some of the macros above, you can disable them individually using Cargo features. The features are:

- `markdown_deps_updated`enables- `assert_markdown_deps_updated`
- `html_root_url_updated`enables- `assert_html_root_url_updated`
- `contains_regex`enables- `assert_contains_regex`- `assert_only_contains_regex`

All of these features are enabled by default. If you disable all
of them, you can still use [ assert_contains_substring](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_contains_substring.html) to
quickly check that a given file contains the current crate
version.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_contains_regex.html)- contains_ - regex
- Assert that versions numbers are up to date via a regex.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_contains_substring.html)- contains_ - substring
- Assert that versions numbers are up to date via substring matching.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_html_root_url_updated.html)- html_ - root_ - url_ - updated
- Assert that the `html_root_url`attribute is up to date.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_markdown_deps_updated.html)- markdown_ - deps_ - updated
- Assert that dependencies on the current package are up to date.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_only_contains_regex.html)- only_ - contains_ - regex
- Assert that all versions numbers are up to date via a regex.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_contains_regex.html)- contains_ - regex
- Check that `path`contain the regular expression given by`template`.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_contains_substring.html)- contains_ - substring
- Check that `path`contain the substring given by`template`.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_html_root_url.html)- html_ - root_ - url
- Check version numbers in `html_root_url`attributes.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_markdown_deps.html)- markdown_ - deps
- Check dependencies in Markdown code blocks.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_only_contains_regex.html)- only_ - contains_ - regex
- Check that `path`only contains matches to the regular expression given by`template`.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# Athena RS 3.25.0

current version: `3.26.3`

## Athena

Athena is the Rust gateway and runtime (core binary: `athena_rs`).

- `athena_rs`— the runtime, server, and library surfaces.
- `athena`— the CLI / toolchain that interfaces the- `athena_rs`runtime and the APIs.

The `athena` CLI is the recommended way to interact with Athena (clients, SQL, pipelines, audit, provisioning, etc.). Just run `athena` with no arguments for a friendly guide.

### Start here

- [Docs hub](https://docs.rs/docs/README.md)
- [Workspace scale](https://docs.rs/docs/workspace-scale.md)
- [Workspace manifest](https://docs.rs/docs/workspace-manifest.md)
- [CLI manifest](https://docs.rs/docs/cli-manifest.md)
- [Crates overview](https://docs.rs/crates/README.md)and- [crate manifest](https://docs.rs/crates/MANIFEST.md)
- [Apps overview](https://docs.rs/apps/README.md)and- [app manifest](https://docs.rs/apps/MANIFEST.md)
- [Benches overview](https://docs.rs/benches/README.md)and- [bench manifest](https://docs.rs/benches/MANIFEST.md)
- [Examples overview](https://docs.rs/examples/README.md)and- [example manifest](https://docs.rs/examples/MANIFEST.md)

### Repository shape

- `src/`holds the root- `athena_rs`server/runtime and the Rust SDK surface.
- `crates/`contains 29 package directories, including 28 root-workspace members and 1 adjacent crate.
- `apps/`contains 8 operator, docs, desktop, marketing, and edge-delivery surfaces.
- `sql/`contains runnable provision and migration SQL.
- `docs/`contains repo-local architecture, runtime, and workspace documentation.
- `openapi.yaml`and- `openapi-wss.yaml`capture the HTTP and WebSocket contracts.

### Common workflows

- Inspect the runtime CLI from the repo root with `cargo run --bin athena -- --help`(or`athena --help`after building).
- Run Rust tests and heavier Rust verification from WSL2 on this machine rather than the Windows toolchain.
- Use the folder READMEs when changing one surface; use the MANIFEST files when you need the whole workspace map.

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scirs-electrochemistry-advanced)SciRS Electrochemistry (Advanced)

Formal modeling of electrochemical systems. No simplified equations.

This crate provides:

- Nernst Equation (Redox potentials, Activity effects)
- Butler-Volmer Kinetics (Overpotential, Exchange current)

# sqlitx 0.1.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sqlitx/0.1.4

# sqlitx

`fzf`-powered connection picker for [sqlit](https://github.com/Maxteabag/sqlit).

## Installation

Requires `fzf` and `sqlit` on `PATH`.

```
```
## Usage

Run `sqlitx` to open an interactive picker over all saved connections. Selecting one runs `sqlit -c "<name>"` in the current shell.

## Design

Connection config is resolved in order:

- `$SQLIT_CONFIG_DIR/connections.json`
- `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/sqlit/connections.json`
- `~/.config/sqlit/connections.json`

sqlitx reads sqlit's connection store directly without spawning sqlit just to list connections. The actual database connection is delegated entirely to the `sqlit` binary. Built in Rust, startup is under 10ms.

# everruns_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-core/0.17.3/everruns_core/

## Expand description

Core agent abstractions for Everruns.

`everruns-core` is the shared contract crate for the
[Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem. It defines the runtime-facing
types used by embedded hosts, workers, provider drivers, integrations, and
the control plane.

The crate is deliberately storage-agnostic. Agent execution is expressed in
terms of traits such as [ MessageRetriever](https://docs.rs/message_retriever/trait.MessageRetriever.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToolExecutor.html)

`ToolExecutor`[, and](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.EventEmitter.html)

`EventEmitter`[, while host crates decide whether those traits are backed by memory, PostgreSQL, gRPC, or another system.](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ProviderStore.html)

`ProviderStore`[§](https://docs.rs#main-surfaces)Main Surfaces

- Agent, harness, session, message, event, and typed ID models
- Capability and tool traits for composing agent behavior
- Provider-neutral LLM messages, streams, and driver registration
- Context assembly for the shared `input -> reason -> act`execution flow
- In-memory helpers and `llmsim`for deterministic tests and examples

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use everruns_core::{CapabilityRegistry, DriverRegistry, PlatformDefinition};
use everruns_core::capabilities::TestMathCapability;
let mut capabilities = CapabilityRegistry::new();
capabilities.register(TestMathCapability);
let platform = PlatformDefinition::new(capabilities, DriverRegistry::new());
assert!(platform.capability_registry().get("test_math").is_some());
```

# pivx_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pivx-rpc/0.4.0/pivx_rpc/

## Expand description

PIVX SDK: typed JSON-RPC client for pivxd with first-class support for shielded (SHIELD/Sapling) balances and transactions.

```
use pivx_rpc::{Auth, PivxClient, ShieldRecipient, ShieldWatcher, WatchOptions};
let client = PivxClient::new(
    "http://127.0.0.1:51473",
    Auth::UserPass { user: "rpcuser".into(), pass: "rpcpass".into() },
)?;
// Watch a shielded address via its viewing key (no spend key needed).
let imported = client.import_sapling_viewing_key("p-view-key...", None, None).await?;
let mut watcher = ShieldWatcher::new(&client, WatchOptions {
    addresses: vec![imported.address],
    ..Default::default()
});
let events = watcher.poll().await?; // first poll primes silently
// Send shielded funds (node wallet holds the keys and builds the proof).
let txid = client
    .shield_send_many(
        pivx_rpc::FromAddress::AnyShield,
        &[ShieldRecipient::new("ps1...", 1.5).with_memo("hello")],
    )
    .await?;
```

# sim_lib_pitch_namer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-namer/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_pitch_namer/

## Expand description

Multi-school cluster naming for the SIM music libraries.

This crate is the aggregator over the pitch-naming schools. It defines the
shared [ ClusterNamer](https://docs.rs/trait.ClusterNamer.html) trait and the

[taxonomy, then drives every built-in school – Forte set-class names, functional roman numerals, plain set-theory prime forms, neo-Riemannian labels, and jazz chord symbols – through one](https://docs.rs/enum.NamingSchool.html)

`NamingSchool`[. The registry can label a pitch-class set in every school at once and translate a label from one school to another. The schools themselves live in the](https://docs.rs/struct.NamerRegistry.html)

`NamerRegistry``sim-lib-pitch-namer-*` sibling crates; this
crate composes them and exposes them as a SIM runtime library through
[/](https://docs.rs/struct.PitchNamerLib.html)

`PitchNamerLib`[.](https://docs.rs/fn.install_pitch_namer_lib.html)

`install_pitch_namer_lib`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cluster](https://docs.rs/struct.ClusterLabel.html)- Label
- A label produced by one naming school for one pitch-class set.
- [Cluster](https://docs.rs/struct.ClusterMeta.html)- Meta
- Metadata attached to a produced `ClusterLabel`
- [Label](https://docs.rs/struct.LabelContext.html)- Context
- The context a namer may use: an optional chord root and an optional key.
- [Namer](https://docs.rs/struct.NamerRegistry.html)- Registry
- A registry of `ClusterNamer`
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/struct.PitchNamerLib.html)- Namer - Lib
- Host-registered lib exporting the built-in cluster-namer cards and registry,
built on the shared `SurfacePackLib`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Naming](https://docs.rs/enum.NamingSchool.html)- School
- A school of chord and pitch-set naming.
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/enum.PitchNamerError.html)- Namer - Error
- Error returned by naming-registry operations.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Cluster](https://docs.rs/trait.ClusterNamer.html)- Namer
- A namer that labels a pitch-class set within one `NamingSchool`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [install_](https://docs.rs/fn.install_pitch_namer_lib.html)- pitch_ - namer_ - lib
- Installs the `PitchNamerLib``cx`, registering each namer’s export record; installing more than once is a no-op.

# facett - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett/0.1.10/facett/

## Expand description

**facett** — umbrella crate. One dependency that re-exports every component,
so a consumer writes `facett::graph::GraphView` / `facett::map::MapView` etc.
instead of pulling each `facett-*` crate. The `Facet` model + the headless
test `harness` are at the root.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [clip](https://docs.rs/clip/index.html)
- **Cross-facet typed copy/paste**(§16) — the trait + payload machinery so copy/paste carries- **full typed data**between facett components, not just text. A process-wide transfer registry holds the last typed- `ClipPayload`
- [effects](https://docs.rs/effects/index.html)
- **effects**— motion + bloom for the facett look. Pure egui,- **glow backend only**: everything here paints with layered alpha shapes on an- `egui::Painter`
- [harness](https://docs.rs/harness/index.html)
- Headless test harness — **fire up a**: its`Facet`, inject data, render it offscreen, and capture what it drew`state_json`+ a vertex count (a “it drew something” proxy) + a stderr activity trail. No display, no GPU. This is the basis of facett’s auto test matrix, and mirrors nornir viz’s`NORNIR_VIZ_STATE`introspection — every component is observable from outside.
- [look](https://docs.rs/look/index.html)
- **facett look & feel**(the work-order architecture, §3) — one- `Theme`- **Windows**,- **macOS**,- **Device**(effects-off, rugged/military). The- `Theme`- *single source of truth*:- `Theme::apply`- `egui::Style`(visuals + spacing + scroll) plus the text scale in one call, and also publishes the derived legacy- `crate::Theme`
- [nav](https://docs.rs/nav/index.html)
- **Shared spatial navigation + focus**(§13 FOC-2, §14 NAV-1) — the- *one*pan/zoom model (- `Navigable`) reused by map/graph/plot/canvas, and the- *one*spatial focus rule (- `nearest_in_direction`) reused by pane and form navigation (COH-3). Pan/zoom is expressed as an- `egui::emath::TSTransform`(scale + offset), so a host can also use it to transform an overlaid guest layer (§5 CMP-4).
- [scroll_](https://docs.rs/scroll_engine/index.html)- engine
- **CygnusEd smooth-scroll engine**(§11) — pixel-by-pixel, sub-pixel soft scrolling with momentum/acceleration, à la the Amiga editor’s jerkyless feel. The scroll- *offset*is decoupled from row height (renderers paint at a- **fractional**pixel offset + clip), and the whole thing is- **deterministic under an injected clock**(- `advance(dt)`), so snapshots reproduce exactly (FC-7 / P0-5). Reusable by text, console, and the dataframe grid (SCRL-3).
- [theme](https://docs.rs/theme/index.html)
- **Theming.**A palette the custom-painted components (graph/depgraph/map) read from the egui context, plus matching egui- `Visuals`for the standard widgets (pop/table/pipeline). Call- `set_theme`- `Theme::default`- `Theme::sci_fi`- `Theme::nordic_aurora`- `Theme::cyberpunk_neon`- `Theme::amber_crt`- `Theme::deep_space`- `Theme::hugin_noir`- `Theme::ALL`- `Theme::by_name`

# facett_map3d_flight - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-map3d-flight/0.1.10/facett_map3d_flight/

## Expand description

**facett-map3d-flight** — the AAA planetary **FLIGHT-SIM** engine layer over the
lightweight, embeddable [ facett_map3d](https://docs.rs/facett-map3d/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_map3d/index.html) map. This crate carries the heavy,
GPU-required, full-screen “bells and whistles”;

`facett-map3d` stays lean
(flat ground + extruded house markers, CPU-fallback, deck-pane-embeddable).[§](https://docs.rs#what-has-landed-here-cpu-foundation--build--test-green-headless)What has LANDED here (CPU foundation — build + test green, headless)

- `origin`- **floating origin**: an- `f64`Web-Mercator world frame + per-frame camera-centred rebase to- `f32`, killing far-from-origin vertex jitter / Z-fighting at planetary scale (FLIGHT-SIM #1).
- `atmos`- **precomputed atmospheric scattering**: a Bruneton/Hillaire-style transmittance LUT + single-scatter sky-view + aerial perspective, feeding both the sky AND the terrain/building haze, varying with altitude + sun angle (FLIGHT-SIM #2). Derived sky tints are ready to drive- `facett_map3d`’s existing analytic- `sky.wgsl`uniforms.
- `camera_fly`- **camera rig**: a deterministic 6DOF state machine (free-fly primary / cinematic orbit / flight-stick) over the- `f64`world frame, exercising the floating origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-roadmapped--spiked-see-nornirflightsim-engine-roadmapmd)What is ROADMAPPED / spiked (see `.nornir/flightsim-engine-roadmap.md`)

GPU scattering-LUT precompute pass, GPU-compute building extrusion (BuildingMeta
marshaller + indirect draw), CDLOD/quadtree DEM terrain + the drape fix, and the
out-of-core Hilbert-sorted GeoParquet streaming. The shared `Mesh3` + wgpu
pipeline + sky/water shaders are **reused** from `facett_map3d` (re-exported
below), not forked.

Everything that lands here is pure CPU math (no GPU, no egui at the foundation layer), so the precision + scattering + rig invariants are directly inject-assert-testable and deterministic (FC-7).

A 3D mesh of the extruded map: positions + per-vertex normals (parallel) +

- [SunSky](https://docs.rs/struct.SunSky.html)

(the seam the scattering plugs into) + the LOD ladder.
A directional sun + sky environment. All colours are linear-ish `[r,g,b]`in`0..1`;`dir`points FROM the surface TO the sun (the convention the PBR shader’s`dot(n, l)`wants).

# xcelerator_solver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xcelerator-solver/0.1.0/xcelerator_solver/

## Expand description

Xcelerator Solver — deterministic, precision-configurable symbolic regression engine.

Given tabular data (CSV) and an explicit vocabulary of allowed terms and operators, the solver exhaustively searches for mathematical expressions that explain the data within a user-specified error threshold.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-principles)Design principles

- **Deterministic**— Bottom-Up Enumeration (BUE) always finds the simplest formula at any error level first. Identical inputs produce identical results.
- **Explicit pool**— only declared terms and operators are used; no hidden defaults, no open-ended constant optimization.
- **Configurable precision**— expressions can be evaluated at arbitrary MPFR precision (- `--features hp`); named constants (- `Pi`,- `e`,- `gamma`, …) are materialized at full target precision via MPFR built-ins.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start-library-usage)Quick start (library usage)

```
use xcelerator_solver::{SolverConfig, solve};
let config = SolverConfig::load("solver.toml".as_ref()).unwrap();
let result = solve(config).unwrap();
```

- Aggregator: bounded top-X heap, error-threshold filter, pinned check.

- TOML configuration loading and validation for the solver.

- Pipeline wiring: owns VisitedSet, spawns threads, connects all actors.

# lipsum 0.9.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lipsum/0.9.1

# Lorem Ipsum

Lipsum is a small Rust library for generating pseudo-Latin [lorem
ipsum filler text](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorem_ipsum). This is a standard placeholder text
used in publishing. It starts with:

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua. Ut enim ad minim veniam, quis nostrud exercitation ullamco laboris nisi ut aliquip ex ea commodo consequat…

The text is generated using a [Markov chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain) that has been trained on
the first book in Cicero's work *De finibus bonorum et malorum* (*On
the ends of good and evil*), of which the lorem ipsum text is a
scrambled subset.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.9"
```
## Documentation

Please see the ** API documentation**.

## Getting Started

Use the `lipsum` function to generate lorem ipsum text:

```
use lipsum;
```
This generates the lorem ipsum text show above:

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua. Ut enim ad minim veniam, quis nostrud exercitation ullamco…

The text becomes random after 18 words, so you might not see exactly the same text.

Use `lipsum_title` instead if you just need a short text suitable for
a document title or a section heading. The text generated by that
function looks like this:

Refugiendi et Omnino Rerum

Small words are kept uncapitalized and punctuation is stripped from all words.

## Release History

This is a changelog with the most important changes in each release.

### Version 0.9.1 (2024-03-13)

- [#100](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/100): Add- `lipsum_title_with_rng`function.
- [#102](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/102): Document MSRV in- `Cargo.toml`.
- [#103](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/103): Enable dependabot updates.

### Version 0.9.0 (2023-03-28)

- [#90](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/90): Test minimum supported Rust version (Rust 1.56) in CI
- [#91](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/91): Remove dependency on system randomness

### Version 0.8.2 (2022-06-06)

- [#84](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/84): Fix build error on Rust 1.56. Thanks @WorldSEnder for the report.

### Version 0.8.1 (2022-04-19)

- [#73](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/73): Add- `lipsum_from_seed`and tweak capitalization. Thanks @reknih!
- [#77](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/77): Update to Rust 2021 edition.

### Version 0.8.0 (2021-05-30)

The random number generator has been separated from the `MarkovChain`
implementation to allow using the same trained model to generate
multiple outputs with different seeds. Thanks @Diggsey!

### Version 0.7.0 (2020-07-08)

-
The code has been updated to the [Rust 2018 edition](https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2018/).
-
Each new release will only support the latest stable version of Rust. Trying to support older Rust versions has proven to be a fool's errand: our dependencies keep releasing new patch versions that require newer and newer versions of Rust.
-
[#65](https://github.com/mgeisler/lipsum/pull/65): A new`lipsum_words_from_seed`function was added. It generates random but deterministic lorem ipsum text. This is useful in unit tests when you need fixed inputs.

### Version 0.6.0 (2018-12-09)

The new `lipsum_words` function can be used to generate random lorem
ipsum text that doesn't always start with "Lorem ipsum".

Dependencies were updated and the oldest supported version of Rust is now 1.22.

### Version 0.5.0 (2018-04-22)

The new `lipsum_title` function can be used to generate a short string
suitable for a document title or a section heading.

Dependencies were updated and the oldest supported version of Rust is now 1.17.

### Version 0.4.0 (2017-09-24)

The `generate` and `generate_from` now always generate proper
sentences, meaning that they generate sentences that start with a
capital letter and end with `.` or some other punctuation character.
Use `iter` and `iter_from` directly if you need more control.

### Version 0.3.0 (2017-07-28)

Performance is improved by about 50% when generating text, but training the Markov chain now takes about twice as long as before.

The `MarkovChain` struct has many new methods:

-
`new_with_rng`makes it possible to specify the random number generator used by the Markov chain. Use this to get deterministic and thus reproducible output for tests.`MarkovChain`now owns the RNG it uses and as a consequence, it has an extra type parameter. This is a breaking change if you used struct directly in your code.
-
`iter`and`into_from`return iterators over words in the Markov chain. The`generate`and`generate_from`methods are now straight-forward convenience wrappers for the iterators.
-
`len`tells you the number of stats in the Markov chain and`is_empty`tells you if the Markov chain is empty, meaning that it hasn't been trained on anything yet.

### Version 0.2.0 (2017-07-10)

Rust version 1.6.0 is now supported. This is checked with TravisCI.

### Version 0.1.0 (2017-07-2)

First public release.

## License

Lipsum can be distributed according to the [MIT license](https://docs.rs/LICENSE).
Contributions will be accepted under the same license.

# lipsum 0.9.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lipsum/0.9.1/source/

#
                    lipsum 0.9.1

                Lipsum is a lorem ipsum text generation library. It generates
pseudo-random Latin text. Use this if you need filler or dummy text
for your application.
The text is generated using a simple Markov chain, which you can
instantiate to generate your own pieces of pseudo-random text.

---

# lipsum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lipsum/0.9.1/target-redirect/lipsum/

## Expand description

Lorem ipsum generator.

This crate generates pseudo-Latin [lorem ipsum placeholder
text](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorem_ipsum). The traditional lorem ipsum text start like this:

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.

This text is in the [ LOREM_IPSUM](https://docs.rs/constant.LOREM_IPSUM.html) constant. Random looking text
like the above can be generated using the

[function. The function allows you to generate as much text as desired and each invocation will generate different text.](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum.html)

`lipsum`The random looking text is generated using a [Markov chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain) of
order two, which simply means that the next word is based on the
previous two words in the input texts. The Markov chain can be
used with other input texts by creating an instance of
[ MarkovChain](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html) and calling its

[method.](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html#method.learn)

`learn`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Markov](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html)- Chain
- Simple order two Markov chain implementation.
- [Words](https://docs.rs/struct.Words.html)
- Never-ending iterator over words in the Markov chain.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [LIBER_](https://docs.rs/constant.LIBER_PRIMUS.html)- PRIMUS
- The first book in Cicero’s work De finibus bonorum et malorum (“On
the ends of good and evil”). The lorem ipsum text in
`LOREM_IPSUM`
- [LOREM_](https://docs.rs/constant.LOREM_IPSUM.html)- IPSUM
- The traditional lorem ipsum text as given in [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorem_ipsum). Using this text alone for a Markov chain of order two doesn’t work very well since each bigram (two consequtive words) is followed by just one other word. In other words, the Markov chain will always produce the same output and recreate the lorem ipsum text precisely. However, combining it with the full text in`LIBER_PRIMUS`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [lipsum](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum.html)
- Generate `n`words of lorem ipsum text. The output will always start with “Lorem ipsum”.
- [lipsum_](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum_title.html)- title
- Generate a short lorem ipsum text with words in title case.
- [lipsum_](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum_title_with_rng.html)- title_ - with_ - rng
- Generate a short lorem ipsum text with words in title case with a custom RNG.
- [lipsum_](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum_with_rng.html)- with_ - rng
- Generate `n`words of lorem ipsum text with a custom RNG. The output will always start with “Lorem ipsum”.
- [lipsum_](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum_words.html)- words
- Generate `n`words of lorem ipsum text.
- [lipsum_](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum_words_with_rng.html)- words_ - with_ - rng
- Generate `n`words of lorem ipsum text with a custom RNG.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Bigram](https://docs.rs/type.Bigram.html)
- A bigram is simply two consecutive words.

[38](https://docs.rs#38)/// Simple order two Markov chain implementation.
[39](https://docs.rs#39)///
[40](https://docs.rs#40)/// The [Markov chain] is a chain of order two, which means that it
[41](https://docs.rs#41)/// will use the previous two words (a bigram) when predicting the
[42](https://docs.rs#42)/// next word. This is normally enough to generate random text that
[43](https://docs.rs#43)/// looks somewhat plausible. The implementation is based on
[44](https://docs.rs#44)/// [Generating arbitrary text with Markov chains in Rust][blog post].
[45](https://docs.rs#45)///
[46](https://docs.rs#46)/// [Markov chain]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain
[47](https://docs.rs#47)/// [blog post]: https://blakewilliams.me/posts/generating-arbitrary-text-with-markov-chains-in-rust
[48](https://docs.rs#48)#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default)]
[49](https://docs.rs#49)pub struct MarkovChain<'a> {
[50](https://docs.rs#50)    map: HashMap<Bigram<'a>, Vec<&'a str>>,
[51](https://docs.rs#51)    keys: Vec<Bigram<'a>>,
[52](https://docs.rs#52)}
[53](https://docs.rs#53)
[54](https://docs.rs#54)impl<'a> MarkovChain<'a> {
[55](https://docs.rs#55)    /// Create a new empty Markov chain.
[56](https://docs.rs#56)    ///
[57](https://docs.rs#57)    /// # Examples
[58](https://docs.rs#58)    ///
[59](https://docs.rs#59)    /// ```
[60](https://docs.rs#60)    /// # fn main() {
[61](https://docs.rs#61)    /// use lipsum::MarkovChain;
[62](https://docs.rs#62)    /// use rand::SeedableRng;
[63](https://docs.rs#63)    /// use rand_chacha::ChaCha20Rng;
[64](https://docs.rs#64)    ///
[65](https://docs.rs#65)    /// let mut chain = MarkovChain::new();
[66](https://docs.rs#66)    /// chain.learn("infra-red red orange yellow green blue indigo x-ray");
[67](https://docs.rs#67)    ///
[68](https://docs.rs#68)    /// let mut rng = ChaCha20Rng::seed_from_u64(0);
[69](https://docs.rs#69)    ///
[70](https://docs.rs#70)    /// // The chain jumps consistently like this:
[71](https://docs.rs#71)    /// assert_eq!(chain.generate_with_rng(&mut rng, 1), "Orange.");
[72](https://docs.rs#72)    /// assert_eq!(chain.generate_with_rng(&mut rng, 1), "Infra-red.");
[73](https://docs.rs#73)    /// assert_eq!(chain.generate_with_rng(&mut rng, 1), "Yellow.");
[74](https://docs.rs#74)    /// # }
[75](https://docs.rs#75)    /// ```
[76](https://docs.rs#76)    pub fn new() -> MarkovChain<'a> {
[77](https://docs.rs#77)        Default::default()
[78](https://docs.rs#78)    }
[79](https://docs.rs#79)
[80](https://docs.rs#80)    /// Add new text to the Markov chain. This can be called several
[81](https://docs.rs#81)    /// times to build up the chain.
[82](https://docs.rs#82)    ///
[83](https://docs.rs#83)    /// # Examples
[84](https://docs.rs#84)    ///
[85](https://docs.rs#85)    /// ```
[86](https://docs.rs#86)    /// use lipsum::MarkovChain;
[87](https://docs.rs#87)    ///
[88](https://docs.rs#88)    /// let mut chain = MarkovChain::new();
[89](https://docs.rs#89)    /// chain.learn("red green blue");
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    /// assert_eq!(chain.words(("red", "green")), Some(&vec!["blue"]));
[91](https://docs.rs#91)    ///
[92](https://docs.rs#92)    /// chain.learn("red green yellow");
[93](https://docs.rs#93)    /// assert_eq!(chain.words(("red", "green")), Some(&vec!["blue", "yellow"]));
[94](https://docs.rs#94)    /// ```
[95](https://docs.rs#95)    pub fn learn(&mut self, sentence: &'a str) {
[96](https://docs.rs#96)        let words = sentence.split_whitespace().collect::<Vec<&str>>();
[97](https://docs.rs#97)        for window in words.windows(3) {
[98](https://docs.rs#98)            let (a, b, c) = (window[0], window[1], window[2]);
[99](https://docs.rs#99)            self.map.entry((a, b)).or_default().push(c);
[100](https://docs.rs#100)        }
[101](https://docs.rs#101)        // Sync the keys with the current map.
[102](https://docs.rs#102)        self.keys = self.map.keys().cloned().collect();
[103](https://docs.rs#103)        self.keys.sort_unstable();
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    }

[253](https://docs.rs#253)    pub fn iter_with_rng<R: Rng>(&self, mut rng: R) -> Words<'_, R> {
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        let initial_bigram = if self.is_empty() {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)            ("", "")

[257](https://docs.rs#257)            *self.keys.choose(&mut rng).unwrap()

[292](https://docs.rs#292)
[293](https://docs.rs#293)/// Never-ending iterator over words in the Markov chain.
[294](https://docs.rs#294)///
[295](https://docs.rs#295)/// Generated with the [`iter`] or [`iter_from`] methods.
[296](https://docs.rs#296)///
[297](https://docs.rs#297)/// [`iter`]: struct.MarkovChain.html#method.iter
[298](https://docs.rs#298)/// [`iter_from`]: struct.MarkovChain.html#method.iter_from
[299](https://docs.rs#299)pub struct Words<'a, R: Rng> {
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    map: &'a HashMap<Bigram<'a>, Vec<&'a str>>,
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    rng: R,
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    keys: &'a Vec<Bigram<'a>>,
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    state: Bigram<'a>,
[304](https://docs.rs#304)}
[305](https://docs.rs#305)
[306](https://docs.rs#306)impl<'a, R: Rng> Iterator for Words<'a, R> {
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    type Item = &'a str;
[308](https://docs.rs#308)
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<&'a str> {
[310](https://docs.rs#310)        if self.map.is_empty() {
[311](https://docs.rs#311)            return None;
[312](https://docs.rs#312)        }
[313](https://docs.rs#313)
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        let result = Some(self.state.0);
[315](https://docs.rs#315)
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        while !self.map.contains_key(&self.state) {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)            self.state = *self.keys.choose(&mut self.rng).unwrap();
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        }
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        let next_words = &self.map[&self.state];
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        let next = next_words.choose(&mut self.rng).unwrap();
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        self.state = (self.state.1, next);
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        result
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)}
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)/// Check if `c` is an ASCII punctuation character.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)fn is_ascii_punctuation(c: char) -> bool {
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    c.is_ascii_punctuation()
[329](https://docs.rs#329)}
[330](https://docs.rs#330)
[331](https://docs.rs#331)/// Capitalize the first character in a string.
[332](https://docs.rs#332)fn capitalize(word: &str) -> String {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    let idx = match word.chars().next() {
[334](https://docs.rs#334)        Some(c) => c.len_utf8(),
[335](https://docs.rs#335)        None => 0,
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    };
[337](https://docs.rs#337)
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    let mut result = String::with_capacity(word.len());
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    result.push_str(&word[..idx].to_uppercase());
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    result.push_str(&word[idx..]);
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    result
[342](https://docs.rs#342)}
[343](https://docs.rs#343)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)/// Join words from an iterator. The first word is always capitalized
[345](https://docs.rs#345)/// and the generated sentence will end with `'.'` if it doesn't
[346](https://docs.rs#346)/// already end with some other ASCII punctuation character.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)fn join_words<'a, I: Iterator<Item = &'a str>>(mut words: I) -> String {
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    match words.next() {
[349](https://docs.rs#349)        None => String::new(),
[350](https://docs.rs#350)        Some(word) => {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)            // Punctuation characters which ends a sentence.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)            let punctuation: &[char] = &['.', '!', '?'];
[353](https://docs.rs#353)
[354](https://docs.rs#354)            let mut sentence = capitalize(word);
[355](https://docs.rs#355)            let mut needs_cap = sentence.ends_with(punctuation);
[356](https://docs.rs#356)
[357](https://docs.rs#357)            // Add remaining words.
[358](https://docs.rs#358)            for word in words {
[359](https://docs.rs#359)                sentence.push(' ');
[360](https://docs.rs#360)
[361](https://docs.rs#361)                if needs_cap {
[362](https://docs.rs#362)                    sentence.push_str(&capitalize(word));
[363](https://docs.rs#363)                } else {
[364](https://docs.rs#364)                    sentence.push_str(word);
[365](https://docs.rs#365)                }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)
[367](https://docs.rs#367)                needs_cap = word.ends_with(punctuation);
[368](https://docs.rs#368)            }
[369](https://docs.rs#369)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)            // Ensure the sentence ends with either one of ".!?".
[371](https://docs.rs#371)            if !sentence.ends_with(punctuation) {
[372](https://docs.rs#372)                // Trim all trailing punctuation characters to avoid
[373](https://docs.rs#373)                // adding '.' after a ',' or similar.
[374](https://docs.rs#374)                let idx = sentence.trim_end_matches(is_ascii_punctuation).len();
[375](https://docs.rs#375)                sentence.truncate(idx);
[376](https://docs.rs#376)                sentence.push('.');
[377](https://docs.rs#377)            }
[378](https://docs.rs#378)
[379](https://docs.rs#379)            sentence
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        }
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)}
[383](https://docs.rs#383)
[384](https://docs.rs#384)/// The traditional lorem ipsum text as given in [Wikipedia]. Using
[385](https://docs.rs#385)/// this text alone for a Markov chain of order two doesn't work very
[386](https://docs.rs#386)/// well since each bigram (two consequtive words) is followed by just
[387](https://docs.rs#387)/// one other word. In other words, the Markov chain will always
[388](https://docs.rs#388)/// produce the same output and recreate the lorem ipsum text
[389](https://docs.rs#389)/// precisely. However, combining it with the full text in
[390](https://docs.rs#390)/// [`LIBER_PRIMUS`] works well.
[391](https://docs.rs#391)///
[392](https://docs.rs#392)/// [Wikipedia]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorem_ipsum
[393](https://docs.rs#393)/// [`LIBER_PRIMUS`]: constant.LIBER_PRIMUS.html
[394](https://docs.rs#394)pub const LOREM_IPSUM: &str = include_str!("lorem-ipsum.txt");
[395](https://docs.rs#395)
[396](https://docs.rs#396)/// The first book in Cicero's work De finibus bonorum et malorum ("On
[397](https://docs.rs#397)/// the ends of good and evil"). The lorem ipsum text in
[398](https://docs.rs#398)/// [`LOREM_IPSUM`] is derived from part of this text.
[399](https://docs.rs#399)///
[400](https://docs.rs#400)/// [`LOREM_IPSUM`]: constant.LOREM_IPSUM.html
[401](https://docs.rs#401)pub const LIBER_PRIMUS: &str = include_str!("liber-primus.txt");
[402](https://docs.rs#402)
[403](https://docs.rs#403)thread_local! {
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    // Markov chain generating lorem ipsum text.
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    static LOREM_IPSUM_CHAIN: MarkovChain<'static> = {
[406](https://docs.rs#406)        let mut chain = MarkovChain::new();
[407](https://docs.rs#407)        // The cost of learning increases as more and more text is
[408](https://docs.rs#408)        // added, so we start with the smallest text.
[409](https://docs.rs#409)        chain.learn(LOREM_IPSUM);
[410](https://docs.rs#410)        chain.learn(LIBER_PRIMUS);
[411](https://docs.rs#411)        chain
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    }
[413](https://docs.rs#413)}
[414](https://docs.rs#414)
[415](https://docs.rs#415)/// Generate `n` words of lorem ipsum text. The output will always start with
[416](https://docs.rs#416)/// "Lorem ipsum".
[417](https://docs.rs#417)///
[418](https://docs.rs#418)/// The text continues with the standard lorem ipsum text from [`LOREM_IPSUM`]
[419](https://docs.rs#419)/// and becomes randomly generated but deterministic if more than 18 words is
[420](https://docs.rs#420)/// requested. See [`lipsum_words`] if fully random text is needed.
[421](https://docs.rs#421)///
[422](https://docs.rs#422)/// # Examples
[423](https://docs.rs#423)///
[424](https://docs.rs#424)/// ```
[425](https://docs.rs#425)/// use lipsum::lipsum;
[426](https://docs.rs#426)///
[427](https://docs.rs#427)/// assert_eq!(lipsum(7), "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing.");
[428](https://docs.rs#428)/// ```
[429](https://docs.rs#429)///
[430](https://docs.rs#430)/// [`LOREM_IPSUM`]: constant.LOREM_IPSUM.html
[431](https://docs.rs#431)/// [`lipsum_words`]: fn.lipsum_words.html
[432](https://docs.rs#432)pub fn lipsum(n: usize) -> String {
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    LOREM_IPSUM_CHAIN.with(|chain| chain.generate_from(n, ("Lorem", "ipsum")))
[434](https://docs.rs#434)}
[435](https://docs.rs#435)
[436](https://docs.rs#436)/// Generate `n` words of lorem ipsum text with a custom RNG. The output will
[437](https://docs.rs#437)/// always start with "Lorem ipsum".
[438](https://docs.rs#438)///

[531](https://docs.rs#531)/// Generate a short lorem ipsum text with words in title case with a custom RNG.
[532](https://docs.rs#532)///
[533](https://docs.rs#533)/// A custom RNG allows to base the markov chain on a different random number
[534](https://docs.rs#534)/// sequence. This also allows using a regular [`thread_rng`] random number
[535](https://docs.rs#535)/// generator. If that generator is used, the text will differ in each
[536](https://docs.rs#536)/// invocation.
[537](https://docs.rs#537)///
[538](https://docs.rs#538)/// The words are capitalized and stripped for punctuation characters.
[539](https://docs.rs#539)///
[540](https://docs.rs#540)/// # Examples
[541](https://docs.rs#541)///
[542](https://docs.rs#542)/// ```
[543](https://docs.rs#543)/// use lipsum::lipsum_title_with_rng;
[544](https://docs.rs#544)/// use rand::thread_rng;
[545](https://docs.rs#545)///
[546](https://docs.rs#546)/// println!("{}", lipsum_title_with_rng(thread_rng()));
[547](https://docs.rs#547)/// ```
[548](https://docs.rs#548)///
[549](https://docs.rs#549)/// This will generate a string like
[550](https://docs.rs#550)///
[551](https://docs.rs#551)/// > Grate Meminit et Praesentibus
[552](https://docs.rs#552)///
[553](https://docs.rs#553)/// which should be suitable for use in a document title for section
[554](https://docs.rs#554)/// heading.
[555](https://docs.rs#555)///
[556](https://docs.rs#556)/// [`thread_rng`]: https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/fn.thread_rng.html
[557](https://docs.rs#557)pub fn lipsum_title_with_rng(mut rng: impl Rng) -> String {
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    LOREM_IPSUM_CHAIN.with(|chain| {
[559](https://docs.rs#559)        let n = rng.gen_range(TITLE_MIN_WORDS..TITLE_MAX_WORDS);
[560](https://docs.rs#560)        // The average word length with our corpus is 7.6 bytes so
[561](https://docs.rs#561)        // this capacity will avoid most allocations.
[562](https://docs.rs#562)        let mut title = String::with_capacity(8 * n);
[563](https://docs.rs#563)
[564](https://docs.rs#564)        let words = chain
[565](https://docs.rs#565)            .iter_with_rng(rng)
[566](https://docs.rs#566)            .map(|word| word.trim_matches(is_ascii_punctuation))
[567](https://docs.rs#567)            .filter(|word| !word.is_empty())
[568](https://docs.rs#568)            .take(n);
[569](https://docs.rs#569)
[570](https://docs.rs#570)        for (i, word) in words.enumerate() {
[571](https://docs.rs#571)            if i > 0 {
[572](https://docs.rs#572)                title.push(' ');
[573](https://docs.rs#573)            }
[574](https://docs.rs#574)
[575](https://docs.rs#575)            // Capitalize the first word and all long words.
[576](https://docs.rs#576)            if i == 0 || word.len() > TITLE_SMALL_WORD {
[577](https://docs.rs#577)                title.push_str(&capitalize(word));
[578](https://docs.rs#578)            } else {
[579](https://docs.rs#579)                title.push_str(word);
[580](https://docs.rs#580)            }
[581](https://docs.rs#581)        }
[582](https://docs.rs#582)        title
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    })
[584](https://docs.rs#584)}

# LOREM_IPSUM in lipsum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lipsum/0.9.1/lipsum/constant.LOREM_IPSUM.html

`pub const LOREM_IPSUM: &`[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html) = "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do\neiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua. Ut enim ad\nminim veniam, quis nostrud exercitation ullamco laboris nisi ut\naliquip ex ea commodo consequat. Duis aute irure dolor in\nreprehenderit in voluptate velit esse cillum dolore eu fugiat nulla\npariatur. Excepteur sint occaecat cupidatat non proident, sunt in\nculpa qui officia deserunt mollit anim id est laborum.\n";## Expand description

The traditional lorem ipsum text as given in [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorem_ipsum). Using
this text alone for a Markov chain of order two doesn’t work very
well since each bigram (two consequtive words) is followed by just
one other word. In other words, the Markov chain will always
produce the same output and recreate the lorem ipsum text
precisely. However, combining it with the full text in
[ LIBER_PRIMUS](https://docs.rs/constant.LIBER_PRIMUS.html) works well.

# lipsum in lipsum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lipsum/0.9.1/lipsum/fn.lipsum.html

## Expand description

Generate `n` words of lorem ipsum text. The output will always start with
“Lorem ipsum”.

The text continues with the standard lorem ipsum text from [ LOREM_IPSUM](https://docs.rs/constant.LOREM_IPSUM.html)
and becomes randomly generated but deterministic if more than 18 words is
requested. See

[if fully random text is needed.](https://docs.rs/fn.lipsum_words.html)

`lipsum_words`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use lipsum::lipsum;
assert_eq!(lipsum(7), "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing.");
```

# MarkovChain in lipsum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lipsum/0.9.1/lipsum/struct.MarkovChain.html

`pub struct MarkovChain<'a> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Simple order two Markov chain implementation.

The [Markov chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain) is a chain of order two, which means that it
will use the previous two words (a bigram) when predicting the
next word. This is normally enough to generate random text that
looks somewhat plausible. The implementation is based on
[Generating arbitrary text with Markov chains in Rust](https://blakewilliams.me/posts/generating-arbitrary-text-with-markov-chains-in-rust).

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lipsum/lib.rs.html#54-284)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-MarkovChain%3C'a%3E)### impl<'a> [MarkovChain](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html)<'a>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lipsum/lib.rs.html#54-284)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-MarkovChain%3C'a%3E)

### impl<'a> [MarkovChain](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html)<'a>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lipsum/lib.rs.html#76-78)#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)() -> [MarkovChain](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html)<'a>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lipsum/lib.rs.html#76-78)

#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)() -> [MarkovChain](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html)<'a>

Create a new empty Markov chain.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use lipsum::MarkovChain;
use rand::SeedableRng;
use rand_chacha::ChaCha20Rng;
let mut chain = MarkovChain::new();
chain.learn("infra-red red orange yellow green blue indigo x-ray");
let mut rng = ChaCha20Rng::seed_from_u64(0);
// The chain jumps consistently like this:
assert_eq!(chain.generate_with_rng(&mut rng, 1), "Orange.");
assert_eq!(chain.generate_with_rng(&mut rng, 1), "Infra-red.");
assert_eq!(chain.generate_with_rng(&mut rng, 1), "Yellow.");
```
Add new text to the Markov chain. This can be called several times to build up the chain.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use lipsum::MarkovChain;
let mut chain = MarkovChain::new();
chain.learn("red green blue");
assert_eq!(chain.words(("red", "green")), Some(&vec!["blue"]));
chain.learn("red green yellow");
assert_eq!(chain.words(("red", "green")), Some(&vec!["blue", "yellow"]));
```
Returs the number of states in the Markov chain.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use lipsum::MarkovChain;
let mut chain = MarkovChain::new();
assert_eq!(chain.len(), 0);
chain.learn("red orange yellow green blue indigo");
assert_eq!(chain.len(), 4);
```
Returns `true` if the Markov chain has no states.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use lipsum::MarkovChain;
let mut chain = MarkovChain::new();
assert!(chain.is_empty());
chain.learn("foo bar baz");
assert!(!chain.is_empty());
```
Get the possible words following the given bigram, or `None`
if the state is invalid.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use lipsum::MarkovChain;
let mut chain = MarkovChain::new();
chain.learn("red green blue");
assert_eq!(chain.words(("red", "green")), Some(&vec!["blue"]));
assert_eq!(chain.words(("foo", "bar")), None);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lipsum/lib.rs.html#188-190)#### pub fn [generate_with_rng](https://docs.rs#method.generate_with_rng)<R: [Rng](https://docs.rs/rand/0.8.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/rng/trait.Rng.html)>(&self, rng: R, n: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lipsum/lib.rs.html#188-190)

#### pub fn [generate_with_rng](https://docs.rs#method.generate_with_rng)<R: [Rng](https://docs.rs/rand/0.8.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/rng/trait.Rng.html)>(&self, rng: R, n: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

Generate a sentence with `n` words of lorem ipsum text. The
sentence will start from a random point in the Markov chain
generated using the specified random number generator,
and a `.` will be added as necessary to form a full sentence.

See [ generate_with_rng_from](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html#method.generate_with_rng_from) if you want to control the
starting point for the generated text and see

[if you simply want a sequence of words.](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkovChain.html#method.iter_with_rng)

`iter_with_rng`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

Generating the sounds of a grandfather clock:

```
use lipsum::MarkovChain;
use rand_chacha::ChaCha20Rng;
use rand::SeedableRng;
let mut chain = MarkovChain::new();
chain.learn("Tick, Tock, Tick, Tock, Ding! Tick, Tock, Ding! Ding!");
println!("{}", chain.generate_with_rng(ChaCha20Rng::seed_from_u64(0), 15));
```
The output looks like this:

Ding! Tick, Tock, Tick, Tock, Ding! Ding! Tock, Ding! Tick, Tock, Tick, Tock, Tick, Tock.
